Gird often appears in formal, literary, or slightly elevated writing. In everyday casual speech, people might say "prepare yourself" or "brace yourself" instead. But gird is not rare or archaic — it appears regularly in journalism, literature, speeches, and formal writing.
How to Distinguish Its Two Meanings at a Glance

When gird refers to something physical (a wall, a belt, a ring of trees), it means to surround or encircle.

When gird refers to a person or their inner state (herself, himself, their courage, their resolve), it means to prepare firmly for something hard.

The context will always make it clear which sense is being used.
Synonyms That Help Anchor the Meaning

For the "encircle" sense: surround, encircle, ring, enclose, border.

For the "prepare yourself" sense: brace, steel, fortify, ready, strengthen.

None of these synonyms are perfect replacements — gird has its own flavor of determined, almost warrior-like readiness — but they can help you feel the territory of the word.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By

Gird = to wrap tightly around something, or to prepare yourself with resolve and determination to face something demanding.

Whenever you see or hear "gird," ask yourself: is something being surrounded? Or is someone bracing for a challenge? One of those two things is always happening — and once you see that, the word will never confuse you again.
6815:
The Simple Meaning First

"Gird one's loins" means to prepare yourself for something difficult, challenging, or demanding that is about to happen. It is a way of saying "get ready" — not just physically, but mentally too. It suggests that what's coming will require real effort, courage, or strength, and you need to be in the right state to face it.

Think of it this way: if someone says "It's time to gird your loins," they're essentially saying "Brace yourself. This won't be easy. Get ready."
Where It Comes From — The Literal Origin

To truly understand this idiom, you need to travel back thousands of years to ancient times — specifically to the world of the Bible and ancient Middle Eastern civilizations.

Back then, people wore long, loose, flowing robes or tunics that reached down to their ankles or shins. These garments were comfortable for everyday life — walking around, resting, going about normal duties. But the moment someone needed to run, fight, do hard physical labour, or move quickly, that long robe became a serious problem. It would tangle around the legs, restrict movement, and slow the person down dangerously.

So, what did they do?

They would grab the hem of the robe, pull it up, and tuck it into their belt — the belt that was tied around their waist and hips. The "loins" simply refers to the area around your hips, waist, and upper thighs — basically your midsection. And "gird" is an old word meaning to encircle, bind, or secure something (it's related to the word "girdle," which is a band worn around the waist).

So "girding your loins" was literally the physical act of tucking up your robe and securing it at the waist so your legs were freed up and you could move fast and freely. It was what a soldier did before battle, what a runner did before a race, what a worker did before heavy labour. It was the ancient equivalent of rolling up your sleeves.

Because "girding the loins" was always done just before a moment of great challenge or intense action, the phrase began to carry the meaning of that preparation itself — the inner act of getting ready. Over time, people stopped using it only in the literal, physical sense and started using it figuratively for mental and emotional preparation as well.

The phrase appears many times in the Bible, which is largely responsible for keeping it alive in the English language. For example, in the Book of Job, God commands Job to "gird up now thy loins like a man," meaning prepare yourself, stand firm, and face what's coming. In the New Testament, believers are told to have their "loins girded" as a symbol of readiness and alertness. These biblical uses cemented the phrase into the English-speaking world for centuries.
What It Feels Like to Use It Today

In modern English, "gird one's loins" is somewhat old-fashioned and formal in tone, but it is very much still used. It often has a slightly dramatic or even humorous flavour because it sounds grand and heroic even when used for everyday challenges. That contrast — using ancient warrior language for ordinary life — is part of its charm.

It can be used in serious contexts (genuinely difficult situations) or in a lighthearted, self-mocking way (overdramatizing a small challenge).

Here are some examples to make the meaning crystal clear:

Serious use:

  • "Before walking into that tough job interview, she took a deep breath and girded her loins."
    She mentally prepared herself for a difficult, high-pressure situation.

Light-hearted / humorous use:

  • "Right, the dishes have been piling up for three days. Time to gird my loins and deal with it."
    Used humorously to treat a small chore as if it were a great battle.

Encouraging someone else:

  • "The meeting with the difficult client is in ten minutes. Gird your loins."
    A way of telling someone to prepare themselves — it won't be comfortable, but face it head-on.

Before a big challenge:

  • "The team girded their loins for the final round of the championship."
    They gathered their focus, courage, and energy before a defining moment.
The Key Feeling Behind the Idiom

What makes this idiom special is the attitude it implies. It doesn't just mean "get ready." It means get ready with a sense of determination and resolve. There's a warrior spirit in it. When you gird your loins, you're not running away from the challenge — you're squaring up to face it. You're acknowledging it will be hard, AND you're choosing to meet it anyway.

It is a phrase of active courage, not passive fear.

These phrases carry a similar meaning and are often used in the same situations:

  • "Brace yourself" — prepare for something unpleasant or difficult.
  • "Steel yourself" — make yourself mentally tough for what's coming.
  • "Roll up your sleeves" — prepare to work hard (also a physical action turned into a metaphor).
  • "Buckle up" — get ready for a rough or intense experience.
  • "Bite the bullet" — endure a painful or difficult situation with courage.

Among all of these, "gird one's loins" is the most literary, biblical, and historically rich, which is why writers, speakers, and storytellers still reach for it when they want their words to carry a certain weight and gravitas.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

ElementDetail

Literal meaning: To tuck up your long robe into your belt so your legs are free to move — done by ancient people before battle or hard work.

Figurative meaning: To prepare yourself — mentally, emotionally, and physically — for something difficult or demanding that lies ahead.

Tone: Formal, slightly old-fashioned, and often used with a touch of drama or humour.

Core feeling: Determined readiness. Not just getting ready — but choosing to face the hard thing.

Once you know the image of an ancient warrior bundling up his robes before battle, the idiom never leaves you. Every time you hear "gird one's loins," you'll see that warrior — and understand that whoever is using the phrase is getting into that same headspace: something tough is coming, and I am ready for it.
6816:
A girder is a large, strong, horizontal beam — typically the most important load-bearing beam in a structure. Its job is to span a wide gap between two supports (like columns, pillars, or walls) and carry the heavy weight above it, then transfer that weight down into those supports at its ends.

Think of a bridge crossing a river. The girder is the long, horizontal steel or concrete member stretching from one pillar to the next. Everything — the road surface, the traffic, the weight of the bridge itself — rests on it. The girder catches all that weight and channels it down into the pillars beneath.

When a heavy load pushes down on the middle of a girder, two forces act on it at the same time. The top of the girder gets compressed — squeezed and pushed together. The bottom of the girder gets stretched — pulled apart under tension. The girder's shape and material are specifically designed to resist both of these forces simultaneously, so it doesn't bend, crack, or collapse.

The most common shape for a steel girder is the I-beam — a cross-section that looks exactly like the capital letter "I" (and sometimes like an "H"). The two wide horizontal plates at the top and bottom are called the flanges, and the vertical plate connecting them in the middle is called the web.

This I-shape is brilliantly efficient. The flanges handle the compression and tension forces, while the web handles shearing (the internal sliding force). Using an I-shape instead of a solid rectangular block gives you near-maximum strength with far less material — which means less weight and lower cost.

That said, girders don't always look like an I. Depending on the type, they can look like a hollow rectangular box, a flat welded plate assembly, or even a large triangular framework.

A plate girder is built by welding three steel plates together — two flanges and one web — forming a custom I-shape. It is used when standard steel I-beams aren't big or strong enough. You'll find these in heavy railway bridges and large highway bridges.

A box girder is shaped like a hollow rectangular box. It is extremely rigid and highly resistant to twisting, which makes it the dominant choice in modern highway bridges, elevated highways, and flyovers. If you've ever looked at the underside of a motorway overpass and seen a deep, rectangular concrete structure running between the supporting columns — that is a box girder.

An I-beam girder (or wide-flange beam) is the standard I-shaped section used widely in building construction. In multi-story buildings, these run horizontally between vertical steel columns to carry the weight of the floors above.

A truss girder is not a single solid beam at all. Instead, it is a rigid framework made of many smaller members arranged in a pattern of triangles. It functions as a girder because it spans a gap and carries loads, but its open triangular framework makes it much lighter than a solid beam of the same length. You'll find truss girders in long railway bridges and large industrial roof structures.

A composite girder is a steel girder bonded to a concrete slab on top of it, so that the two materials behave as one unified unit. The concrete carries the compression; the steel carries the tension. This combination is highly efficient and is widely used in modern bridge construction.

A concrete girder is made entirely of reinforced or prestressed concrete. In reinforced concrete girders, steel rods (called rebars) are embedded inside the concrete — the concrete handles compression, and the steel handles tension. In prestressed concrete girders, steel cables inside the beam are put under tension before the load is even applied, which pre-compresses the concrete and allows it to carry much heavier loads over longer spans.

Structural steel is the most common material for girders in large bridges and industrial buildings. It is strong in both tension and compression.

Reinforced concrete (concrete with embedded steel bars) is extremely common in building construction and highway infrastructure. It is cheaper than steel and very durable.

Prestressed concrete is used where even greater strength is needed, such as in long-span highway bridges and railway bridges. The pre-tensioning process dramatically improves its load-carrying capacity.

Timber (wood) is used in smaller, lighter structures such as houses, small wooden bridges, and agricultural buildings. A large solid or engineered wood beam can serve perfectly well as a girder at the domestic scale.

Girders are everywhere once you know what to look for.

In bridges, girders are the primary structural elements spanning between the piers or abutments, carrying the road or rail track above. In buildings, steel girders span horizontally between columns on every floor, forming the skeleton that holds the structure up. In highway overpasses and flyovers, you are essentially looking at a series of concrete girders supported on columns every time you drive under one. In warehouses and factory buildings, long-span girders allow wide, open floor spaces without columns interrupting the middle of the building. In bridge cranes and overhead gantry cranes, the horizontal travelling beam that carries the hoisting hook is itself a girder — the crane rolls along it.
How Girder Differs from Similar Words

Girder vs. Beam: A beam is the broad, general term for any horizontal structural member that carries loads by bending. A girder is a specific kind of beam — usually the largest and most important primary beam in a structure, which itself supports the smaller secondary beams resting on it. Every girder is a beam, but not every beam is a girder. Girders sit at the top of the hierarchy.

Girder vs. Joist: A joist is a smaller, lighter, closely-spaced beam that rests on top of a girder (or on a wall). Joists run perpendicular to the girder and directly support the floor or roof decking above them. They transfer their load down onto the girder below. Think of the girder as the primary beam and the joists as the secondary beams sitting on it.

Girder vs. Column / Pillar: A column (or pillar) is vertical — its job is to carry load straight down into the foundation. A girder is horizontal — its job is to span across a gap and transfer load to the columns at its ends. Girders rest on top of columns. Together, columns and girders form the fundamental structural skeleton of most large buildings and bridges.

Girder vs. Truss: A truss is a rigid framework made of many smaller members joined in triangular patterns. A truss can function as a girder (in which case it's called a truss girder), but a girder itself is often a single solid or plate-built beam. The distinction is about form: a girder is typically a solid or hollow beam, while a truss is always an open framework.

Girder vs. Rafter: A rafter is a sloped structural member used in pitched roof construction. Girders are horizontal (or nearly so) and are the primary load carriers in floors, bridges, and flat roofs. Rafters are sloped and specific to roof framing.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Think of a girder as the backbone of a structure's horizontal framework. Just as your spine carries the load of your upper body and distributes it downward through your hips and legs, a girder carries the load bearing down on it and channels it to the vertical supports at its two ends.

The next time you drive under a highway overpass, look up. Those large, deep rectangular or I-shaped members you see running between the concrete columns — spanning the gap from one column to the next and holding up the road above — are girders. That image is the word made real.
6817: A girdle is anything that goes all the way around something, like a ring, band, or belt encircling an object. Think of it like a hug that wraps completely around a thing. Every specific meaning of this word grows out of this one central image — something that encircles.

1. A Belt or Band Worn Around the Waist

The most classic meaning of girdle is a belt, sash, or cord tied or fastened around a person's waist. Historically, both men and women wore girdles to hold their clothing in place, carry pouches or weapons, or simply as decoration. Soldiers, priests, monks, and royalty all wore some form of girdle throughout history. It was an everyday item, the way we think of a belt today.

Think of a rope tied around the middle of a robe to keep it from flowing open — that rope is a girdle.

2. A Woman's Supportive Undergarment

In more modern usage (especially the 20th century), a girdle came to refer to a tight, elastic undergarment worn by women around the waist, stomach, hips, and sometimes upper thighs. Its purpose was to shape, firm, and smooth the figure — compressing and supporting the midsection beneath clothing. It sits somewhere between a corset (which is rigid and laces up) and modern shapewear. Unlike a corset, a girdle is flexible and made of elastic or stretchy fabric.

If you've heard of Spanx or control-top shapewear today, a girdle is the older ancestor of those garments.

3. Anything That Encircles or Surrounds Something

In a more general, descriptive sense, girdle is used as a word for anything that forms a ring or band around something else. Writers and poets especially use it this way.

"A girdle of mountains surrounded the valley." — Here, the mountains form a complete ring around the valley, like a belt.

"The ancient city had a girdle of stone walls for protection." — The walls go all the way around the city.

This is a beautiful, expressive use of the word — whenever something wraps around something else completely, you can call it a girdle.

4. In Anatomy — The Shoulder Girdle and Hip Girdle

In the science of the human body, girdle has a very precise meaning: it refers to a ring-shaped arrangement of bones that connects the limbs (arms or legs) to the main skeleton (the spine and torso).

There are two:

  • The Pectoral Girdle (Shoulder Girdle): This is the set of bones — the collarbone (clavicle) and the shoulder blade (scapula) — that forms a partial ring at your shoulders and connects your arms to your body. It is called a "girdle" because these bones curve around the top of your chest like a band.
  • The Pelvic Girdle (Hip Girdle): This is the complete ring of bones at your hips — the two large hip bones on the sides and the sacrum at the back — that connects your legs to your spine. It forms a full, closed ring, like a bony belt around your lower torso.

In both cases, the bones form a "belt-like" structure around part of the body — hence the name girdle.

5. In Gemology — The Girdle of a Cut Gemstone

When a gemstone (like a diamond) is cut and polished, it has different sections. The girdle is the thin, outermost rim around the widest part of the stone — the narrow band that divides the top half (called the crown) from the bottom half (called the pavilion). It is essentially the "equator" of the gemstone.

The girdle is important because it is the part that a ring or jewellery setting grips to hold the stone in place. Gem cutters pay careful attention to the girdle — if it is too thin, the stone can chip; if it is too thick, it adds unnecessary weight and looks bulky.

Imagine slicing a diamond horizontally at its widest point — the edge of that slice is the girdle.

6. In Trees — A Ring-Shaped Wound

In the world of botany and forestry, a girdle refers to a complete ring of damage cut into the bark of a tree trunk or branch. When the bark is removed all the way around a tree (in a full circle), it disrupts the flow of nutrients and water between the roots and leaves, and can eventually kill the tree or branch above the cut. This ring of damage — the wound itself — is called a girdle.

You may have seen a tree that has had its bark stripped all the way around its trunk in a band — that stripped ring is a girdle. Insects, animals, or humans can create girdles on trees.

7. A Flat Cooking Plate (Scottish / Northern English)

In Scotland and parts of northern England, a girdle (also sometimes spelled griddle) is a flat, circular iron plate used for cooking over a fire or on a stove. It is used to bake things like oatcakes, scones, and flatbreads directly on the hot surface without an oven. The round shape of the plate is what connects it to the broader idea of a girdle.

Scottish girdle scones are a classic example — baked right on this flat iron pan.

Every single meaning of girdle traces back to the same core idea: a band, ring, or belt that wraps around something. Whether it is:

  • a belt around your waist,
  • elastic fabric shaping a woman's figure,
  • mountains encircling a valley,
  • bones looping around your shoulders or hips,
  • the rim encircling a gemstone,
  • a ring of damaged bark around a tree, or
  • a round iron plate,

...the connecting thread is always the idea of something circular or encircling.

Once you see that, the word girdle becomes very easy to recognise and understand in any context you encounter it.
6818:
A girl is a female human being who is young — typically a child or a teenager who has not yet become an adult. This is the word's most basic and straightforward use.

For example:

  • A newborn female baby is a girl.
  • A five-year-old female child is a girl.
  • A sixteen-year-old female teenager is a girl.

This is not a sharp, fixed line. It shifts based on context, culture, and even the speaker's personal sense of things. As a general guide:

  • Up to around 17–18 years old → almost always called a girl.
  • 18 and older → generally called a woman, though girl is still widely used in informal speech (more on this below).
  • Around 13–17 → either word might be used depending on context.

The word woman is the grown-up, adult equivalent of girl, just as boy and man are the male equivalents. When you want to be precise and respectful about an adult female human, woman is the safe and correct choice.

In everyday, casual conversation, girl is very commonly used to refer to adult women too — and this is perfectly normal and widely accepted in informal contexts. You will encounter this constantly in real life.

Common examples:

  • "I'm going out with the girls tonight." (= female friends, who may all be adults)
  • "She's a smart girl." (said admiringly about a grown woman)
  • "The girls in the office planned the party." (= female colleagues)
  • "You go, girl!" (an encouraging phrase directed at a woman)
  • "Girls' night out" (a social outing among female friends)

In these cases, girl carries a warm, casual, friendly tone. It signals informality and closeness rather than anything negative.

However, context matters a lot. If a person in authority (like a male boss) calls his adult female employees "girls" in a professional setting, it can sound dismissive or disrespectful — as if he doesn't see them as full adults. So while girl is fine in casual, friendly speech among peers, using it for adult women in formal or professional settings can be seen as condescending.

A parent often calls their female child their girl, regardless of her age:

  • "She has two girls and one boy." (= two daughters)
  • "My girl just started university." (= my daughter)

This is a common and natural use.
"Girl" Used for a Female Friend or Romantic Partner (Informal)

In informal speech, girl can also refer to:

  • A close female friend: "She's my girl — we've known each other for years."
  • A girlfriend (romantic partner): "He's been with his girl for two years now."

These uses are casual and affectionate in tone.
Words Related to "Girl" — and How They Differ

Understanding girl fully means knowing how it sits among similar words:

WordMeaning in brief
WomanAn adult female human; the formal/neutral grown-up version of girl
LadyA polite, formal, or refined way to refer to a woman
FemaleA biological/technical term; refers to the sex, not the age
GalAn informal, casual American-English word for a girl or woman
LassA regional (British/Scottish) word for a girl or young woman

These fixed phrases are used very often in English, and knowing them will help you understand the word more fully:

  • "Girl next door" — used to describe an ordinary, wholesome, approachable young woman; someone who seems friendly and down-to-earth rather than glamorous or intimidating.
  • "Old girl" — in British English, an affectionate term for an older woman, or an alumna of a school.
  • "Baby girl" — a newborn female infant; also used affectionately by parents or partners for any female they care for deeply.
  • "Good girl" — an expression of praise, often said to a child who has done something right (or playfully to a well-behaved dog).
  • "Tomboy" — a girl who prefers activities, clothes, or behavior typically associated with boys; not a negative label, just descriptive.
  • "Schoolgirl" — a girl who attends school.
  • "Working girl" — a woman who is employed; note that in some older or slang contexts this phrase can carry different meanings, so be careful with it.
  • "Girl talk" — casual conversation between female friends, especially about personal or social matters.
  • "Girl boss" — informal term for a successful, ambitious woman in a leadership position.
  • "Big girl" — used to encourage a young girl to be brave or mature: "Be a big girl — you can do it!"
  • "Girl crush" — when a woman admires another woman very much (not necessarily in a romantic way).

• In formal writing (official documents, news articles, academic writing): girl is used only for minors; adult women are called women.
  • In informal speech and casual writing (conversations, texts, social media): girl freely applies to women of any age, and carries a friendly, familiar tone.
  • The plural "girls" in casual speech almost always means a group of female friends, regardless of actual age.

The use of girl for adult women has been discussed and debated — some people feel it can minimize or belittle adult women by comparing them to children. Others use it freely with no such intention, simply as warm, casual language. As a learner, the safest rule is:

  • Use girl for female children and teenagers without any worry.
  • Use girl for adult women only in casual, friendly contexts — not in formal, professional, or official situations.
  • When in doubt about an adult female, woman is always the correct and respectful choice.

Girl = a young female human being (child or teenager) in its core meaning, but also widely and casually used for adult women in informal speech to suggest warmth, friendliness, or closeness. It is the female equivalent of boy, and its adult counterpart is woman.
6819:
Imagine you have a big tree in front of you. You want to measure how thick it is — but not by cutting through it and measuring across. Instead, you wrap a measuring tape all the way around the outside of the trunk, like giving it a hug, and you read the number. That measurement — the distance all the way around something — is its girth.

In its simplest terms: girth is how much something measures when you go around it, not across it.

1. A Measurement of Roundness or Thickness (The Common Meaning)

Girth is used to describe the size of something by measuring around its widest or thickest point. It tells you how big around something is.

This is most commonly used for:

The human body — A person's girth usually refers to the measurement around their waist or belly. If someone says a person is "of great girth," they mean the person is large or heavy. It is an honest, somewhat formal way of describing body size.

Trees — The girth of a tree is how far around the trunk is. A tree with a wide girth is an old, massive tree. You might need several people holding hands to wrap around a tree with a very large girth.

Animals — The girth of a horse, for example, is the measurement around its belly, just behind its front legs.

Objects — Any round or thick object can have a girth. A thick pipe, a log, a barrel — if you measure around it, that's its girth.

Think of it this way: Width tells you how far something goes from left to right. Girth tells you how far something goes all the way around. They are not the same thing.

2. A Strap That Goes Around a Horse's Belly (The Specific/Literal Meaning)

In the world of horse-riding, a girth is also the name of a physical object — a wide strap or band, usually made of leather or a strong fabric, that is fastened around a horse's belly to keep the saddle firmly in place on its back. Without the girth, the saddle would slide off.

This is where the measurement meaning originally comes from — the strap wraps around the horse's middle, which is also the "around" part of the animal.

You will mainly come across this meaning if you read about horse-riding, farming, or historical texts.
How Girth Differs from Similar Words

This is important, because learners often confuse girth with similar words.

Girth vs. Circumference — These are very close in meaning. Circumference is the precise, mathematical term for the distance around a circle or round shape. Girth is the more everyday, physical term. You would use circumference in a geometry class, and girth when talking about a real object in the real world — a tree, a person, an animal.

Girth vs. Width — Width is measured straight across something (from one side to the other in a straight line). Girth is measured around something (following the outer surface all the way). A very wide object will likely have a large girth too, but they are measured differently.

Girth vs. Size — Size is general and vague. Girth is specific — it only refers to the measurement around something, not its height, length, or overall volume.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

Girth carries a quiet sense of bigness. When people use this word, they are almost always talking about something substantial, thick, or large. You would not describe a pencil's girth — you would describe a tree trunk's girth. You would not describe a child's girth — you might describe a wrestler's girth.

It is a neutral, non-offensive word, but it does imply size. When used about a person, it is matter-of-fact rather than unkind — it is a measurement, not a judgment.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

• Girth = the measurement all the way around something, especially its thickest or widest part.
  • Think: wrapping a tape measure around a tree trunk, a belly, or a barrel.
  • In horse-riding, a girth is also the name of the strap that holds the saddle around the horse's belly.
  • It is different from width (across) and close to circumference (around a circle), but more physical and everyday.
  • The word almost always implies something is notably large or thick.
6820: Gist means the central meaning or most important point of something — the core of what is being said, written, or communicated, once all the details, examples, and surrounding information have been stripped away.
The simplest way to understand it

Imagine you sat through a one-hour meeting at work. Afterward, your colleague who missed it asks, "What was it about?" You don't replay the entire meeting word for word. You say, "Basically, the company is cutting costs and some jobs may be at risk." That condensed, essential message — the heart of what the meeting was really about — is the gist.

Or imagine someone gives you a long, complicated explanation. You may have forgotten the statistics, the examples, and the minor side points, but you walked away understanding what they were really trying to say. You have the gist. And crucially, that is enough.
How it sounds in real speech

"What's the gist of the article?" → Tell me the main point without going into all the details.

"I didn't read the whole report, but I got the gist of it." → I understood the core message even without reading everything.

"The gist of his argument was that the government spends too much." → The central claim he was making, boiled down to its essence.

"Give me the gist — I don't have time for the full story." → Skip the details; just tell me the most important part.

The most common expression is "get the gist" (to understand the main point) and "give someone the gist" (to tell them the main point).

Gist is not a full summary. A summary can carry several points, facts, or events. The gist is narrower — it is the single essential idea, the beating heart of the whole thing. If someone summarizes a 300-page novel, they might mention the key characters, major plot events, and the ending. But the gist of the novel might simply be: "A man discovers his entire life has been built on a lie and must rebuild his identity from scratch." Everything else in the book supports that idea, but that one sentence is the gist.

Gist is also not about perfect accuracy on every detail. When you say "I got the gist," you're saying you understand the core of something — not that you remember every specific fact. There is a natural looseness to it. You have enough understanding to grasp the essence, even if the finer points escaped you.
How it compares to similar words

Essence is the closest in meaning. The essence of something is its most fundamental, defining quality. You can often swap the two words, but "essence" tends to sound more formal and philosophical — "the essence of democracy is freedom" — whereas "gist" is more conversational and tied to communication specifically.

Crux refers to the most decisive or critical point — the point on which everything else depends, often the trickiest part of an argument or problem. The gist is the central meaning; the crux is the most pivotal part. They're close, but not identical.

Upshot refers to the final result or conclusion of something that happened — "the upshot was that we lost the deal." Gist is about the central meaning of something communicated; upshot is about the end result of something that occurred.

Point is the most casual near-synonym — "what's the point?" feels almost identical to "what's the gist?" But "point" often implies purpose or intention, while "gist" implies the core substance of what was expressed.

The word "gist" almost always refers to something communicated — something said, written, argued, or expressed. You talk about the gist of a speech, an article, a conversation, an argument, a letter, or a book. You wouldn't naturally talk about the "gist of a sunset" or the "gist of a river" — those aren't communications. Gist lives in the world of language and meaning.
The complete picture in one sentence
The gist is what something really means or really says — the irreducible core of a message, once everything non-essential has been cleared away.
6821: Give means to transfer something from yourself to someone else, voluntarily. That "something" can be a physical object, an experience, an action, information, or even something abstract like love or hope. The key idea is: you have it → you move it toward someone else.

1. Hand over a physical object

The most basic use. You take something you have and put it in someone else's possession.

  • She gave him the keys.
  • Give me your phone.
  • He gave the waiter his plate.

2. Give as a gift or donation

You transfer something without expecting it back.

  • My mother gave me a watch for my birthday.
  • They give money to the poor every year.
  • He gave his old clothes to charity.

Note: When you give something, the other person keeps it. This is different from lend, where you expect it back.

3. Pay a price

When you exchange money for something.

  • I'll give you five hundred rupees for that book.
  • What will you give me for this painting?

4. Cause someone to experience something

Here, nothing physical is transferred — instead, you cause a feeling, a condition, or an experience in someone.

  • The news gave her great joy.
  • That smell gives me a headache.
  • His kindness gave me hope.
  • The cold gave him a fever. (transmitted)
  • The teacher gave the students a lot of work.

This is one of the most important uses. "Give" here means to be the source of something someone experiences.

5. Perform an action (Give + Action Noun)

This is a very common pattern in English. Instead of using a verb directly, we use "give" + a noun made from that verb. The meaning is almost the same, but it often sounds more natural or casual.

PhraseWhat it means
  • Give a speech = speak formally to an audience
  • Give a smile = smile
  • Give a laugh = laugh
  • Give a kick = kick
  • Give a shout = shout
  • Give a try / give a shot = try
  • Give a look = look at
  • Give a call = call someone on the phone
  • Give a hug = hug
  • Give a thought = think about something
  • Give birth = deliver a baby (said of the mother)
  • Give a performance = perform
  • Give a party = host a party

These are extremely common in everyday English. Instead of saying "She smiled at me," people often say "She gave me a smile" — it feels warmer and more personal.

6. Provide, produce, or emit

Here, a thing (not a person) is the subject that "gives."

  • The sun gives light and warmth.
  • The tree gives shade in summer.
  • This plant gives a beautiful fragrance.
  • The engine gives 200 horsepower.

In this sense, "give" means to be a source or to supply something naturally.

7. Communicate or deliver information

  • Give me the details.
  • She gave him directions to the station.
  • The doctor gave her some advice.
  • Give me an answer by tomorrow.
  • The police gave a warning.
  • He gave me the impression that he was unhappy. (= he made me feel that)

8. Grant or allow

  • Give me permission to leave.
  • Give her a chance.
  • Give him some time.
  • The court gave him three years in prison.
  • Give me some space. (= allow me room/freedom)

9. Dedicate or devote

  • She gave her life to science.
  • He gives all his energy to his work.
  • She gave years of service to the company.
  • Give it your full attention.

Here, what you "give" is your time, effort, or life — you direct it completely toward something.

10. Yield or flex under physical pressure

Here the subject is a surface or structure that bends or softens.

  • The mattress gives when you sit on it. (it's soft, it compresses)
  • The ice gave under his weight. (it cracked/moved)
  • The old floorboard gives a little. (it bends slightly)

11. Collapse, fail, or stop working

  • The bridge gave way. (collapsed)
  • Her knees gave out after the long run. (stopped functioning)
  • His voice gave out by the end of the speech. (he lost his voice)
  • My patience finally gave out. (was completely used up)

12. Attribute or assign

  • Give her the credit she deserves.
  • Don't give me the blame for this.
  • They gave the street a new name.
  • Give the project a title.

13. Estimate or predict

  • I give it two weeks before it breaks.
  • How long would you give this relationship? (= how long do you think it will last?)

Understanding how to construct sentences with "give" is essential.

Pattern 1 — give + person + thing (most common)
The recipient comes first, then what is given.

  • Give me the pen.
  • She gave him a hug.
  • They gave the children a holiday.

Pattern 2 — give + thing + to + person
Same meaning, different order. "To" connects the object to the recipient.

  • Give the pen to me.
  • She gave a hug to him.
  • They gave a holiday to the children.

Both patterns mean the same thing. Pattern 1 is more common in speech. Pattern 2 is used when you want to emphasize who is receiving, or when the object is long.

Pattern 3 — give + thing (no recipient mentioned)

  • She gave generously. (gave money/help)
  • He gave a speech.
  • The charity gives every year.

These are verb + preposition combinations where the meaning changes significantly. These are extremely important to know.

Give up
This has several related meanings:

  • Stop trying; admit defeat: I give up — I can't solve this puzzle.
  • Quit a habit: He gave up smoking last year.
  • Surrender yourself to authorities: The criminal gave himself up to the police.
  • Lose hope in someone/something: Don't give up on her — she's trying.

Give in
To yield to someone after resisting; to stop fighting and accept.

  • He refused for weeks, but finally gave in.
  • Don't give in to pressure.
  • She gave in and let them stay up late.

Note the difference: give up often means quitting an effort entirely. Give in usually means you've been resisting something (a request, pressure, temptation) and you finally agree.

Give away
Four distinct meanings:

  1. Give something for free: They're giving away free samples outside the store.
  2. Accidentally reveal a secret: Don't give away the ending of the movie.
  3. Reveal someone's location or identity (unintentionally): His nervous expression gave him away.
  4. Give a bride away at a wedding: Her father gave her away.

Give back
To return something to its owner.

  • Give back the money you borrowed.
  • It's time to give back to the community. (do something good for society)

Give out
Three meanings:

  1. Distribute to multiple people: The volunteers gave out food to the homeless.
  2. Stop working; fail: The old car's engine finally gave out.
  3. Become exhausted or run out: My energy gave out halfway through the hike.

Give off
To emit or release something (heat, light, smell, sound) — usually something you can sense.

  • The candle gives off a soft, warm light.
  • That cheese gives off a very strong smell.
  • The engine gives off a lot of heat.

Give over to
To dedicate something entirely to a purpose.

  • The afternoon was given over to rest.
  • The room was given over to storage.

Give way
Three meanings:

  1. Collapse or break: The old bridge gave way under the truck's weight.
  2. In traffic, yield to other vehicles: Give way to pedestrians at the crossing.
  3. Be replaced by something: Winter gave way to spring. / Her anger gave way to sadness.

Give rise to
To cause something (usually a problem, feeling, or situation) to come into existence.

  • The government's decision gave rise to protests.
  • The damp walls gave rise to mold.
  • His success gave rise to jealousy among his colleagues.

Give someone a hand
Two meanings:

  1. Applaud: Let's give her a hand for that wonderful performance!
  2. Help: Can you give me a hand with this heavy box?

Give someone a break

  1. Stop being harsh: Give him a break — he's just learning.
  2. Give someone an opportunity: All she needs is one person to give her a break.

Give and take
The natural compromise and flexibility in any healthy relationship or negotiation.

  • Every good friendship needs give and take.
  • Marriage requires a lot of give and take.

Give someone the benefit of the doubt
When you're not sure whether someone did something wrong, you choose to assume they didn't.

  • He was late again, but I'll give him the benefit of the doubt.

Give someone a piece of your mind
To speak to someone very directly and angrily about what they did wrong.

  • When she found out, she gave him a piece of her mind.

Give or take
Used to say that a number is approximate — a little more or a little less.

  • The journey takes three hours, give or take.
  • It costs five thousand rupees, give or take a few hundred.

Give someone credit
To acknowledge that someone did something well or deserves recognition.

  • Give credit where credit is due.
  • I'll give him credit — he worked very hard.

What gives?
An informal expression meaning: What's happening? What's wrong? Why is this the way it is?

  • You seem upset. What gives?

Don't give up on someone/something
Keep having hope or faith in that person or thing.

  • Don't give up on your dream.
  • She never gave up on her students, even the difficult ones.

Give it a go / give it a shot / give it a try
All mean the same: attempt something, especially something new or uncertain.

  • I've never cooked Thai food before, but I'll give it a go.

Give someone the cold shoulder
To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly to someone.

  • Ever since the argument, she's been giving me the cold shoulder.

Give a damn (or "give a hoot," "give a toss," etc.)
To care about something. Almost always used in the negative.

  • I don't give a damn what people think.
  • He doesn't give a hoot about rules.

Give someone hell
To punish or scold someone very harshly.

  • Her parents gave her hell for coming home so late.

Give vs. Lend
When you give, the person keeps it permanently. When you lend, you expect it back.

  • I gave him my old jacket. (he keeps it)
  • I lent him my jacket. (I want it back)

Give vs. Offer
When you offer, you present something and the person can accept or refuse. When you give, the transfer actually happens.

  • She offered me tea, but I said no.
  • She gave me tea. (I received it)

Give vs. Send
Give is usually direct, face-to-face, in person. Send is from a distance.

  • Give him this letter when you see him.
  • Send him this letter by post.

Give vs. Donate
Donate is specifically for charitable purposes. Give is broader and works in all situations.

  • She donated her kidneys. (formal, charitable)
  • She gave her kidneys. (also acceptable, more neutral)

Give vs. Take (opposites)
Give is the action of the person who transfers. Take is the action of the person who receives or removes.

  • I gave her the book. (from my side)
  • She took the book from me. (from her side)

"Give" does not follow normal rules to form its past tense.

  • Base form: give (I give, they give)
  • Third person singular present: gives (she gives, he gives)
  • Present participle: giving (I am giving)
  • Past tense: gave (I gave, she gave)
  • Past participle: given (I have given, it was given)

"Given" is especially important in passive sentences:

  • The award was given to her. (passive)
  • He has been given a second chance.

"Given" is also used as an adjective meaning specified or particular:

  • At any given time, thousands of planes are in the air.
  • Given the circumstances, he made the right decision. (= considering the circumstances)

"Give" is about transfer and provision — moving something (an object, an experience, an action, information, a quality) from a source to a recipient. The source is almost always doing this voluntarily. What is "given" can be concrete (a book, money) or entirely abstract (hope, trouble, a smile, your life). The word is one of the most flexible in English, and mastering its phrasal verbs — especially give up, give in, give away, give out, and give off — will unlock a large part of natural, everyday English.
6822:
To give a wide berth to someone or something means to deliberately stay far away from them — to avoid them carefully and by a comfortable distance.

It is not a casual or accidental avoidance. It implies that you are making a conscious choice to keep away — usually because the person, place, or thing is dangerous, unpleasant, troublesome, or simply not worth the bother.

Think of it this way: imagine someone walking toward you on a footpath who is shouting angrily. You don't just step one inch to the side — you cross to the other side of the street entirely to stay as far away as possible. That is giving them a wide berth.

This idiom was born at sea, centuries ago, and it has a beautifully logical origin.

In the world of sailing and ships, a berth is a word for the space around a ship. When sailors said a ship had its "berth," they meant the physical area it occupied on the water.

When a large ship, or a dangerous obstacle like a rocky coastline or a reef, was nearby, an experienced captain would order the crew to steer the ship to keep a wide berth — meaning a large, generous gap between their ship and the hazard. The wider the gap, the safer the ship. There was no "just about enough" — a wise captain gave extra space as a precaution.

Over time, people began borrowing this nautical image and using it in everyday life, beyond ships and oceans. By the 17th and 18th centuries, people were saying "give a wide berth" about anything they wanted to deliberately avoid. Today, it has completely shed its sea legs and lives entirely as a common idiom in daily language.

The idiom is very flexible. You can use it for:

People — someone rude, aggressive, toxic, dishonest, or simply someone whose company you don't enjoy.

Places — locations that are dangerous, crime-prone, unpleasant, or unwise to visit.

Things and situations — risky investments, bad habits, unhealthy foods, confrontational topics, or anything you'd rather not get involved with.

Animals — a stray dog that looks aggressive, a wild animal in the forest, an angry bull in a field.

The idiom can be used in two directions:

  • You can say it as advice to someone else: "Give that man a wide berth."
  • You can say it as a description of what someone did: "She gave the argument a wide berth."

It works comfortably in both spoken and written English, in informal conversations as well as slightly more formal writing. It is not slangy, and it is not stuffy — it sits right in the middle, which makes it very useful.

Here are plenty of examples so you can see exactly how it is used in real situations:

  • "That dog has been barking and growling at everyone. Give it a wide berth."
    → Stay well away from the dog.
  • "After their falling out, Jake and his former business partner gave each other a wide berth at every industry event."
    → They carefully avoided each other.
  • "Tourists are advised to give that part of the city a wide berth at night."
    → Don't go there; it's not safe.
  • "I always give spicy food a wide berth — it just doesn't agree with me."
    → He avoids spicy food deliberately.
  • "She could see the conversation was heading toward politics, so she gave the topic a wide berth and changed the subject."
    → She steered away from a touchy subject.
  • "The new employee quickly learned to give the grumpy supervisor a wide berth on Monday mornings."
    → He avoided the supervisor at that particular sensitive time.
  • "Give cryptocurrency speculation a wide berth if you can't afford to lose that money."
    → Avoid it; it's too risky.

This idiom carries a tone of wisdom or caution, not cowardice. When you say someone "gave something a wide berth," you are usually implying that they were smart to do so — that the thing being avoided was genuinely worth avoiding. It suggests that the avoidance was prudent, sensible, and deliberate.

It is not the same as saying someone ran away in panic or was afraid. It is calmer and more strategic than that. The image is of a confident sailor calmly steering the ship around a hazard, not fleeing from it in terror.

• It does not mean ignoring someone emotionally (like giving someone the "cold shoulder").
  • It does not mean a short or slight detour. The word wide is key — it suggests a generous, deliberate distance, not just a small side-step.
  • It is not rude or offensive to use. Saying "I'd give him a wide berth" is perfectly polite in conversation.

The idiom appears in a few slightly different forms, all meaning the same thing:

  • "Give a wide berth to..." — the most standard form.
  • "Give something a wide berth" — equally common, just reordered.
  • "Steer clear of..." — a different idiom but with the same nautical flavour and the same meaning.
  • "Keep a wide berth from..." — used occasionally, though less standard.

Core meaningTo deliberately stay well away from someone or something
OriginNautical — the safe space kept around a ship at sea
ToneWise, cautious, deliberate
Used forPeople, places, situations, animals, things
RegisterNeutral — fits both casual and formal speech

The next time you hear someone say "give that a wide berth," picture a great sailing ship calmly and wisely steering around a jagged reef — not because the captain is afraid, but because a smart navigator knows exactly what to avoid and gives it plenty of room.
6823:
When someone gives as good as they get, it means they respond to whatever is done to them — an attack, a criticism, a challenge, a competition — with equal strength, skill, or force. They don't shrink back. They don't stay silent. They don't let the other person "win" by default. Instead, they match the other person blow for blow, word for word, or move for move.

In the simplest possible terms: whatever you throw at me, I'll throw right back at you — just as hard.
Breaking Down the Words

Sometimes the easiest way to understand an idiom is to look at what its individual words are doing.

  • "Give" — to send back, to return, to respond with action.
  • "As good" — of the same quality, the same strength, the same level.
  • "As one gets" — as what one receives; as what is being directed at you.

Put it together: Return something of equal quality to what you are receiving. The word "good" here doesn't mean "kind" or "nice." It means effective, strong, or capable — like when we say someone is "good at fighting" or a product is "good quality." So "give as good as you get" really means: be just as capable in your response as the person coming at you.
The Core Idea Behind It: Reciprocity + Strength

This idiom is built on two powerful human instincts:

  1. Reciprocity — the natural impulse to respond in kind to what you receive.
  2. Self-respect and toughness — the refusal to be a pushover or to simply absorb whatever someone dishes out without responding.

When you "give as good as you get," you are essentially saying: "I am not weaker than you. I will not be dominated. If you come at me with force or skill, I will match it."

This is why the phrase carries a tone of admiration or respect. Saying someone "gives as good as they get" is a compliment. It means they are tough, capable, and unintimidated.
How It Is Used in Real Life

This idiom is used in a wide variety of situations. Here are the most common ones:

1. Arguments and Verbal Sparring
If someone is sarcastic, witty, sharp-tongued, or critical toward you, and you respond with equal sharpness, humour, or comebacks — you are giving as good as you get.

"She may have started the argument, but he gave as good as he got — she didn't expect him to have such sharp comebacks."

2. Sports and Physical Competition
When a weaker or underestimated competitor matches a stronger one punch for punch, tackle for tackle, or point for point.

"The young boxer gave as good as he got against the champion, leaving the crowd stunned."

3. Business Negotiations
When one party in a negotiation refuses to be pushed around and fights back with equally tough terms and tactics.

"Our team was up against a very aggressive legal firm, but our lawyer gave as good as she got."

4. Everyday Conflict or Teasing
Among friends, siblings, or colleagues, when teasing or banter goes back and forth equally.

"My sister always teases me, but I give as good as I get — she knows better than to expect me to stay quiet."
What It Does NOT Mean

It's worth being clear about what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean being aggressive or picking fights. The phrase only applies when someone responds to something — it is reactive, not proactive. The person "gives as good as they get" only because something was first directed at them.
  • It does not mean escalating or going further than what you received. It means matching — being equal, not excessive.
  • It does not suggest revenge or malice. The tone is one of balance and strength, not hatred.
The Tone and Register

This is an informal, everyday expression. You will hear it in casual conversation, in sports commentary, in journalism, and in fiction. It is not a formal or academic phrase. It suits:

  • Spoken English and dialogue
  • Newspaper sports reporting
  • Everyday storytelling
Common Variations of the Phrase

The idiom appears in several closely related forms. All mean the same thing:

  • "Give as good as you get" — the most common everyday form.
  • "Give as good as one gets" — a slightly more formal version using "one" instead of "you."
  • "Give back as good as one gets" — with "back" added for extra emphasis on the returning nature of the action.
Similar Expressions (and How They Differ)

Understanding how this idiom compares to similar ones will sharpen your understanding:

"Tit for tat" — This also means responding to something with an equal action, but it leans more toward petty retaliation, almost like keeping score. "Give as good as you get" sounds more admirable and strong; "tit for tat" can sometimes sound childish.

"Fight fire with fire" — This means using the same tactics as your opponent to defeat them. It is a specific strategy; "give as good as you get" is more about matching energy and force in general.

"An eye for an eye" — This is more about justice and revenge — specifically, that punishment should equal the crime. "Give as good as you get" is broader and not necessarily about punishment.

"Hold your own" — This means managing to survive or compete successfully against someone. It is close in spirit but less aggressive. You can "hold your own" by simply not losing; but "giving as good as you get" means actively fighting back with equal force.
The Opposite of This Idiom

Knowing the opposite of an expression helps lock in its meaning:

  • "Turning the other cheek" — accepting what is done to you without responding.
  • "Rolling over" — submitting without resistance.
  • "Being a pushover" — letting others dominate you without pushing back.

If someone turns the other cheek, they absorb the hit and do nothing. If someone gives as good as they get, they hit right back.
A Quick Memory Trick

If you ever forget the meaning, remember this logic:

You GET something (a hit, an insult, a challenge). You GIVE something back of equal quality. So you GIVE AS GOOD AS YOU GET.

The phrase is almost a perfect description of itself once you see it this way.
Summary in One Sentence

"Give as good as one gets" means to respond to whatever is directed at you — whether an attack, criticism, or competition — with equal force, skill, or sharpness, showing that you are just as strong and capable as the person challenging you.
6824:
To give credence to something means to believe it, or to accept it as true and worthy of trust.

Think of "credence" as simply meaning belief or trust. So when you "give credence to" something, you are giving your belief to it — you are deciding it is real, valid, or trustworthy.
The Word "Credence" — Where It Comes From

Understanding the root of the word makes the idiom stick in your memory forever.

"Credence" comes from the Latin word credere, which means "to believe." This same Latin root gave us many English words you already know:

  • Credible — something believable
  • Incredible — something unbelievable (literally: "cannot be believed")
  • Credentials — proof that makes you worth trusting
  • Credit — trust given to someone financially
  • Creed — a system of beliefs

So the entire family of these words is built on the idea of believing or trusting. "Credence" is simply the noun form — it is the belief itself. When you give credence, you are handing over your trust or belief to something.
Two Slightly Different Ways It's Used

This idiom works in two directions, and both are very common. This is important to understand.

Direction 1 — A Person Gives Credence to Something

Here, a person (or a group of people) is choosing to believe something.

Structure: [Someone] gives credence to [a claim, idea, or theory]

Examples:

  • "I don't give credence to rumors."
    → I do not believe rumors. I don't trust them.
  • "She refused to give credence to his excuses."
    → She did not accept his excuses as true or valid.
  • "Many people gave credence to the scientist's warnings."
    → Many people believed the scientist's warnings were real and serious.

In this use, it describes an active mental choice — a person deciding whether or not to believe something.

Direction 2 — Something Gives Credence to Something Else

Here, a piece of evidence, a fact, or an event makes another thing seem more believable. No person is directly doing the believing — instead, one thing is strengthening the believability of another.

Structure: [Something] gives credence to [a claim, idea, or theory]

Examples:

  • "The eyewitness testimony gives credence to his story."
    → The witness's account makes his story more believable and supported.
  • "The discovery of ancient tools gives credence to the theory that humans lived here thousands of years ago."
    → The discovery supports and validates that theory.
  • "His pale face and shaking hands gave credence to his claim of feeling sick."
    → His physical appearance made his claim of illness seem more believable.

In this use, think of it as one thing lending its weight to another — making it stand more firmly.
The Tone and Register of This Idiom

This is a formal and slightly elevated idiom. You would more commonly see or hear it in:

  • Journalism and news articles
  • Academic writing
  • Formal speeches or debates
  • Serious conversations about evidence, theories, or claims

In casual everyday conversation, people would more often simply say "I believe it" or "that supports it." So if you use this idiom, it gives your language a polished, educated quality.
The Negative Form — Very Common and Important

One of the most frequent ways this idiom appears is in the negative, especially with the word "don't" or "no."

  • "I don't give credence to this nonsense." → I simply don't believe it.
  • "We should give no credence to unverified claims." → We should not believe things that haven't been proven.
  • "Don't give credence to everything you read online." → Don't blindly believe everything online.

When used negatively, the phrase becomes a polite but firm way of dismissing something — saying it is not worth believing.

You will very often see the phrase "lend credence to" instead of "give credence to." They mean exactly the same thing. The only difference is the verb:

  • Give credence to → you are giving/granting belief
  • Lend credence to → you are lending/adding support to believability

Both are correct and interchangeable. "Lend credence to" is arguably even more common in formal writing when talking about evidence supporting a theory.

"The data lends credence to the hypothesis."
"The data gives credence to the hypothesis."

Both sentences are identical in meaning.
Words That Mean the Same Thing (Synonyms)

Depending on context, these phrases carry a similar meaning:

  • Give weight to — very similar; implies something is taken seriously
  • Lend credibility to — almost identical in meaning
  • Validate — to confirm something is true or acceptable
  • Support — to back up a claim
  • Corroborate — especially when evidence confirms something
  • Vouch for — to personally confirm something is trustworthy
  • Substantiate — to provide proof for a claim

If "give credence to" means to believe or support something, the opposites include:

  • Discredit — to damage the believability of something
  • Cast doubt on — to make something seem less believable
  • Dismiss — to reject something as unworthy of belief
  • Debunk — to expose something as false
  • Undermine — to weaken the support for something
Quick Summary You Can Always Return To

MeaningTo believe something, or to make something seem more believable
RootLatin credere = to believe
Used by a person"I give credence to her theory." = I believe her theory.
Used by evidence"This gives credence to her theory." = This makes her theory more believable.
Common negative use"Don't give credence to gossip." = Don't believe gossip.
Twin phrase"Lend credence to" = exactly the same meaning
ToneFormal, polished, educated

If you ever forget the meaning, just remember:

Credence = Belief. To "give" it = to hand it over.

When you give credence to something, you are handing your belief over to it. When something gives credence to a theory, it is handing believability over to that theory.

That's the whole idiom — elegant, precise, and now completely yours.
6825:
To give free rein to someone or something means to allow complete freedom — to let a person, feeling, idea, or process go in any direction it wants, without controlling, limiting, or interfering with it.

Think of it this way: when you give free rein to someone, you are stepping back and saying, "Do what you want. I won't stop you or restrict you."

Examples:

  • The art teacher gave her students free rein to paint whatever they liked.
  • He gave free rein to his imagination and wrote a wildly creative story.
  • The CEO gave the new team free rein to redesign the entire product.

In each case, someone is being allowed to act freely, without rules or restrictions being imposed on them.
Where This Idiom Comes From (The Origin)

This idiom comes directly from horse riding, and understanding that makes the meaning crystal clear forever.

A rein (plural: reins) is the long leather strap that a horse rider holds in their hands. The reins are connected to the horse's bit (a piece in its mouth). By pulling or tightening the reins, the rider controls the horse — its speed, its direction, everything. The horse goes where the rider wants it to go.

Now, when a rider loosens or releases the reins — when they give the horse "free rein" — the horse is no longer being controlled. It can run in any direction, at any speed, as it pleases. It has total freedom of movement.

So the idiom borrows this image perfectly: just as a horse with free rein can move without restriction, a person given free rein can act without restriction.

This is one of the most commonly misspelled idioms in English, so pay close attention.

The correct spelling is: "free rein" ✅

Many people incorrectly write: "free reign" ❌

Here is why this mistake happens: reign (spelled R-E-I-G-N) is a completely different word. It means the period during which a king or queen rules — for example, "during the reign of Queen Elizabeth." It sounds identical to rein but means something entirely different.

The idiom has nothing to do with kings or queens. It is about horse reins, so the correct spelling is always R-E-I-N.

A simple way to remember: think of the horse every time you use this phrase. A horse has reins, not a reign.

The idiom has a very consistent structure. Here are the two main patterns:

Pattern 1: give + [someone/something] + free rein

  • She gave her children free rein in the kitchen.
  • The manager gave the designers free rein.

Pattern 2: give free rein + to + [someone/something]

  • She gave free rein to her emotions.
  • The director gave free rein to his creative instincts.

Both patterns mean the exact same thing. The only difference is word order.

You can also extend it with "to do something":

  • They gave him free rein to make all the decisions.
  • The company gave her free rein to hire whoever she wanted.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom is neutral in itself — it is neither always positive nor always negative. The feeling it carries depends entirely on the context.

When used positively, it suggests trust, empowerment, creativity, and confidence in someone:

  • The coach gave the young player free rein to express herself on the field. (positive — freedom to shine)
  • Parents who give their children free rein to explore nature raise curious, independent thinkers. (positive — healthy development)

When used negatively or with concern, it suggests a lack of control over something that perhaps should have been controlled:

  • The government gave corporations free rein to pollute rivers without any consequences. (negative — harmful freedom)
  • Giving that committee free rein was a mistake — they went completely off track. (negative — poor judgment)

So the idiom itself is simply a description of freedom being granted. Whether that freedom was a good thing or a bad thing is shown by the rest of the sentence.
Its Opposite: "Keep a Tight Rein On"

Because this idiom comes from horse riding, it has a natural opposite expression — "keep a tight rein on" — which means to control something or someone very strictly, without giving much freedom.

  • The strict principal kept a tight rein on student behavior.
  • She kept a tight rein on her spending throughout the month.

Together, these two idioms form a perfect pair on opposite ends of a spectrum: "free rein" (total freedom) vs. "tight rein" (strict control). Knowing both helps you use either one more powerfully.

If you want to say the same thing in different words, these phrases carry a very similar meaning:

  • Give someone a free hand — allow someone to act independently without direction
  • Give carte blanche to — give unconditional freedom or authority (from French, literally meaning "blank paper" — like signing a blank check)
  • Give someone latitude — allow some degree of freedom (slightly softer and more formal)
  • Let someone do as they please — plain, direct way to say the same thing
  • Unleash — a more dramatic word suggesting the release of a powerful force

MeaningTo allow complete freedom; to remove restrictions
OriginHorse riding — loosening the leather reins so the horse can move freely
Correct spellingFree rein (not "reign")
Used forPeople, emotions, ideas, imagination, creativity, forces
ToneNeutral — can be positive (empowering) or negative (reckless), depending on context
OppositeKeep a tight rein on (to control strictly)

The next time you see or hear this phrase, picture a rider relaxing their grip on the reins, and a horse running freely wherever it chooses. That one image holds the entire meaning of the idiom.
6826:
To give ground means to back down, yield, or retreat from a position you were holding — whether that position is physical, in a debate, in a negotiation, or in any kind of conflict or disagreement.

When you give ground, you are accepting a weaker or lesser position than the one you started with. You stop pushing forward and allow the other side to advance or win some of the argument.

Think of it like this: imagine two people in a tug-of-war. If one person starts being pulled forward and loses their footing, they are giving ground — they are losing the space they had.
Where It Comes From — The Origin

The idiom is military in origin, and it is centuries old.

In ancient and medieval warfare, armies literally fought over land — the physical ground beneath their feet. If enemy soldiers pushed your army backward, your army was forced to give up the territory it was standing on. That territory was called ground, and surrendering it was called giving ground.

So a general might report: "We gave ground near the river — we were pushed back three miles."

Over time, people began using this military image as a metaphor for any situation where someone retreats, backs off, or stops resisting — even if no actual land or battle is involved.
How the Meaning Expanded — The Figurative Use

Once the idiom moved from battlefields into everyday language, "ground" stopped meaning physical land. It started meaning:

  • A position you hold in an argument
  • A belief or opinion you stand by
  • A demand you make in a negotiation
  • A boundary you set in a relationship

And "giving" it means letting go of it, relaxing it, or abandoning it — usually because of pressure from the other side.
The Important Nuance — It Is Not Total Surrender

This is a key point that many learners miss.

Giving ground is not the same as completely giving up. There is a subtle but important difference:

SituationWhat It Looks Like
  • Giving ground = You were asking for a 30% discount in a negotiation. Under pressure, you agree to accept 15%. You backed off partly.
  • Surrendering/Capitulating = You walk away with no discount at all. You gave in completely.

Giving ground is a partial retreat, not total defeat. It means you moved back, but you haven't necessarily lost everything. This is why it is often described as a strategic retreat — sometimes, smart negotiators or leaders give ground on purpose to protect something more important.
When Do People Use It?

This idiom appears in many different contexts:

1. Debates and arguments
When someone is being challenged hard but refuses to change their view, you say they refuse to give ground. Conversely, if they start agreeing with parts of the opposing argument, they are giving ground.

"Even after two hours of debate, the professor refused to give ground — she stood by every word of her theory."

2. Negotiations (business, legal, political)
In any negotiation, both sides push and pull. If one side starts agreeing to terms they initially rejected, they are giving ground.

"The union eventually gave ground on the overtime rules, but held firm on the salary issue."

3. Personal relationships and conflicts
When someone in an argument admits they were wrong, changes their stance, or softens their position to keep the peace, they are giving ground.

"After days of fighting, he finally gave ground and admitted that she had a point."

4. Competition and sports (figurative)
A player or team that is being dominated and losing their advantage can be said to be giving ground.

"The champion gave ground in the final rounds as his opponent grew stronger."

5. Politics and social issues
Politicians and parties are often described as giving ground when they shift their policies under public or political pressure.

"The government gave ground on the tax proposal after widespread public protests."
The Grammar — How to Use It Correctly

"Give ground" follows a very consistent grammatical pattern. Here are the structures you need:

a) Give ground (to someone)

"He gave ground to his rivals."
"She refused to give ground to anyone."

b) Give ground on (something)

"They gave ground on the deadline but not on the price."
"The negotiator gave ground on minor issues to protect the bigger deal."

c) Refuse to / not give ground
This is actually the most common use of the idiom. Very often, it is used in the negative — to describe someone who is being stubborn or resilient.

"Despite enormous pressure, the scientist refused to give ground on her findings."
"The prime minister would not give ground, no matter what the opposition said."

d) Past tense: gave ground

"The company eventually gave ground after weeks of protests."
Real-World Example Sentences

Here are varied, natural-sounding sentences to show you the idiom in action:

  1. "The CEO was known for being tough — he never gave ground in a negotiation, no matter how long it took."
  2. "After reviewing the new evidence, the detective gave ground and admitted the original suspect might be innocent."
  3. "In the chess match of political maneuvering, giving ground on a small issue sometimes helps you win the bigger battle."
  4. "She had always stood by her belief that honesty was the best policy, and she wasn't about to give ground now."
  5. "The army gave ground steadily, retreating toward the city walls as the enemy advanced." (used both literally and figuratively)
  6. "His confidence in his own ideas was so total that he gave ground to nobody — which made him both admirable and infuriating."
Related Expressions You Should Know

These expressions are either similar in meaning, opposite in meaning, or closely related. Knowing them will help you understand "give ground" even more deeply.

Synonyms (similar meaning):

  • Back down — to withdraw from a position; slightly more informal
  • Give way — to yield or stop resisting; can be used literally and figuratively
  • Cave in / cave — to give in under pressure; informal and implies weakness
  • Yield — a formal word meaning to give way or concede
  • Concede — to admit that something is true, or to give up a point
  • Capitulate — to surrender, usually after long resistance; stronger than "give ground"
  • Back off — to become less aggressive or insistent; informal

Antonyms (opposite meaning):

  • Hold your ground / stand your ground — to refuse to retreat; to maintain your position firmly (the direct opposite of "give ground")
  • Stand firm — to remain strong and refuse to change
  • Dig in / dig your heels in — to become even more determined not to give way
  • Hold fast — to stay strong; slightly old-fashioned

The most important pair to remember:

Give ground ↔ Hold/Stand your ground

These two expressions are direct opposites and are very commonly used together or in contrast.

"Everyone expected the government to give ground, but it chose to stand its ground instead."
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Some learners confuse "give ground" with "lose ground."

They are related but not the same:

  • Give ground = You choose to yield, or you yield because of pressure. It has an element of agency — something is happening in an active confrontation. It is more dynamic.
  • Lose ground = You are gradually falling behind or declining in strength, popularity, or advantage — often without a direct opponent forcing you. It is more about a trend.

"The company lost ground in the market over three years" (sales slowly declined).
"The company gave ground in the negotiation and accepted a lower price" (they yielded under pressure in a specific moment).

Both phrases involve retreating from a position, but "give ground" is more about a moment of yielding in conflict, while "lose ground" is more about a gradual decline.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

"Give ground" is a neutral-to-slightly-negative idiom in tone. Giving ground is generally seen as a sign of:

  • Weakness (if done too easily or too often)
  • Wisdom or strategy (if done deliberately and tactically to gain something bigger)
  • Fairness or humility (if done after realizing you were wrong)

Context decides which interpretation applies. The same act of "giving ground" can be admired or criticized depending on why it happened.
Quick Summary — Everything in One Paragraph

"Give ground" is an idiom that originated in military warfare, where armies literally surrendered physical territory to the enemy. Today, it means to back down, yield, or retreat from a position — whether in an argument, a negotiation, a competition, or any kind of confrontation. It usually implies partial retreat, not total surrender. It is most commonly used with "refuse to" (e.g., "she refused to give ground"), and it appears in debates, politics, business, and personal conflicts. Its direct opposite is "hold/stand your ground." It is slightly different from "lose ground," which describes a gradual decline rather than an active act of yielding. Depending on context, giving ground can be seen as weak, strategic, or humble.
6827:
"Give rise to" means to cause something to happen, to exist, or to appear — especially something new.

When Thing A gives rise to Thing B, it means Thing A is the reason Thing B exists or happened. Thing A is the cause, and Thing B is the result.

Think of it this way: when the sun rises in the morning, it comes up from below into existence. "Give rise to" borrows that same image — one thing brings something else up into existence.
A Simple Way to Visualize It

Imagine you plant a seed in the ground. That seed gives rise to a plant. The seed is the cause. The plant is the result — it rose up because of the seed.

Now apply that same logic to any situation in life:

Poverty gave rise to crime in that region.

Here, poverty is the "seed" (the cause), and crime is the "plant" (the result that grew out of it).
The Grammar of "Give Rise To"

Understanding the grammar will help you use this idiom correctly every time.

The fixed structure is:

[Cause] + give rise to + [Result/Effect]

The phrase always takes a noun or a noun phrase after it. It never takes a verb directly.

The verb give changes its form depending on the tense:

  • Present: gives rise to / give rise to
  • Past: gave rise to
  • Present Perfect: has/have given rise to
  • Future: will give rise to
  • Passive: was/were given rise to (rare — more on this below)

The subject of the sentence is always the cause — the thing responsible for producing the result.
Examples Across Different Situations

Reading many examples is the best way to truly feel how an idiom works. Pay attention to how the cause always comes before the phrase, and the result always comes after it.

1. Causing a feeling or emotion:

His long absence gave rise to a lot of worry among his friends.

(His absence → caused → worry)
